chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting started on social media

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What social media is and which app does what
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Pick the social media app that fits what you want to do.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you want to do, such as see family photos or find a job, you will choose the social media app that fits it, matching the right app every time.
Social media apps let people share words, photos and videos and talk to each other. Each one is good for different things.
Facebook: family, friends, local groups and events. Instagram: photos and short videos. WhatsApp: free messages and calls with family, also across countries. YouTube: videos to watch and learn from. TikTok: short videos. LinkedIn: jobs and work contacts. Nextdoor: news from your neighborhood.
You do not need all of them. Start with one that matches what you want, such as seeing family photos or finding a job. Each app sets a minimum age in its rules; check them before a child or teen signs up.
Words to know:
- Social media: apps and websites where people share posts and talk to each other.
- Post: something you share: words, a photo or a video.
- Feed: the list of posts you scroll through.
Try it now: Write down one thing you want from social media (for example: see the grandchildren's photos, join a church or community group, or find work). Next to it, write the app from this lesson that fits best.
You can now say what the main social media apps are for and choose one that fits your goal.

check.q: Which app is mainly for news from your neighborhood?
check.why: Nextdoor is for news from your neighborhood.

check.q: You want to see your grandchildren's photos and join a local church group. Which app would you start with?
check.why: Facebook is for family, friends, local groups and events; start with one app that fits.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting up a safe profile
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create an account and fill in a profile without oversharing.
This lesson builds toward: Using a social media app from the official store, you will create an account with a safe profile and turn on two-step verification, with no home address, birth year or phone number on the profile and two-step verification on.
Install the app only from the official app store, or go to the company's real website. Sign up with your email or phone number and a strong password you use nowhere else.
Your profile is the page that tells people who you are. Add your name and a friendly photo. Leave out your birthday year, home address, phone number and when you are away from home. Scammers collect these details.
Turn on two-step verification (sometimes called two-factor authentication) in the app's security settings. Then, even if someone steals your password, they also need a code from your phone.
Step by step:
- Install the app from the official app store.
- Sign up with email or phone and a new, strong password.
- Add your name and a friendly photo.
- Leave out your address, phone number, full birth date and travel plans.
- Open security settings and turn on two-step verification.
Words to know:
- Profile: your page that shows who you are on the app.
- Two-step verification: a second check, usually a code sent to your phone, when you sign in.
Try it now: Create an account on the app you picked (or open the one you have). Check your profile: remove anything from the "leave out" list, and turn on two-step verification.
You can now make a social media profile that shows who you are without giving away private details.

options: The page that tells people who you are
A list of posts from others
check.why: Your profile is your page, with your name and photo.

check.q: The sign-up asks for your full birthday, address and phone to show on your profile. What would you do?
options: Show all of them so people can find you
Leave them off your profile, because scammers collect these details
check.why: Leaving out your birth year, address and phone number protects you from scammers.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Following, posting and commenting
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow people and groups, write a post and leave a kind comment.
This lesson builds toward: On your social media account, you will follow people and groups you have checked, write a post and leave a kind comment, checking who can see each post before you share it.
To see someone's posts, send a friend request or follow them. Search for their name, check the photo and shared friends to be sure it is really them, and tap Add friend or Follow. You can also join groups: a church, a neighborhood, a hobby or a job group.
To post, tap the box that asks what is on your mind, or the + button. Write a few words, add a photo if you like, check who can see it, and tap Post or Share.
Reacting (like a thumbs up or heart) shows you saw a post. Commenting adds your words under it. Be kind: write as if the person were in the room. Remember that what you post can be copied and seen for a long time.
Step by step:
- Search for a person or group by name.
- Check it is the real one: photo, shared friends, posts.
- Tap Add friend, Follow or Join.
- To post: tap the post box or +, write, add a photo, check who can see it, then Post.
- To comment: tap Comment under a post, write something kind, send.
Words to know:
- Follow: choose to see someone's posts in your feed.
- Group: a space on the app for people with the same interest.
- Comment: words you write under someone's post.
- React: tap a like, heart or other symbol on a post.
Try it now: Follow one family member or friend and join or follow one local group or page. Then leave a kind comment on one of their posts.
You can now follow people and groups, make a post, and react and comment kindly.

check.q: What does a reaction, such as a thumbs up or heart, show?
options: That you want to block the person
That you shared the post with everyone
check.why: A reaction shows you saw a post; a comment adds your words.

check.q: You disagree with a cousin's post. What would you do?
options: Write kindly, as if the person were in the room, or say nothing
Write an angry comment in capital letters
Share the post with an insult
check.why: Be kind; what you post can be copied and seen for a long time.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Privacy settings: choosing who sees what
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set your posts and profile so only people you choose can see them.
This lesson builds toward: In the app's privacy settings, you will set who can see your posts, find you and message you, with posts set to friends or approved followers and location in posts turned off.
Every app has privacy settings. They decide who can see your posts, who can find you, and who can message you. Public means anyone in the world. Friends or followers you approve means only people you said yes to.
Look for Settings, then Privacy (on some apps it is in a menu with three lines or your profile picture). Many apps also have a privacy check-up that walks you through each choice.
A good start: make posts visible to friends only, approve new followers yourself, and limit who can message you. Turn off location sharing in posts if you do not want people to know where you are.
Step by step:
- Open the app's menu or your profile picture.
- Choose Settings, then Privacy (or a privacy check-up).
- Set who can see your posts to friends or approved followers.
- Set who can message you and find you.
- Turn off location in posts if you do not need it.
Words to know:
- Public: anyone, even strangers, can see it.
- Privacy settings: the choices that control who sees your posts and profile.
- Location sharing: showing where you are when you post.
Try it now: Open your app's privacy settings. Set your posts to friends or approved followers only, and turn off location in posts. Then look at your own profile the way a stranger would, if the app lets you.
You can now set your privacy so only people you choose see your posts and details.

options: A tool in many apps that walks you through each privacy choice
check.why: Many apps offer a privacy check-up that walks you through each choice.

check.q: You do not want strangers to see where you are when you post. What would you do?
options: Turn off location sharing in posts
check.why: Turning off location in posts stops people knowing where you are.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spotting fake accounts and scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize a fake account or scam message and refuse it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a friend request or message, you will identify the signs of a fake account or scam and refuse it, naming at least two warning signs and never sending money, gift cards or codes.
Scammers make fake accounts, sometimes copying a real friend's name and photo. A second friend request from someone you are already friends with is a warning sign. Ask the real person by phone before you accept.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) lists signs of a scam: pretending to be someone you know or trust, a problem or a prize, pressure to act right now, and asking for payment by gift card, wire transfer, payment app or cryptocurrency. On social media this looks like "You won! Pay a small fee", romance messages that soon ask for money, and "too good to be true" job or investment offers.
Never send money, gift cards or codes to someone you have only met online. In the United States you can report scams at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Be careful with new friend requests, especially from people you already know.
- Check by phone or in person before you accept.
- Watch for: a prize, a rush, money or gift card requests, and love or job offers that turn to money.
- Do not click their links or send money or codes.
- Report the account in the app, and in the US at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Fake account: a profile made by a scammer, often copying a real person.
- Romance scam: a scammer pretends to love you online, then asks for money.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
- FTC: Report fraud
Try it now: Look at your friend requests or followers. For any you are not sure about, check the profile for warning signs. Decline anyone you cannot confirm is real.
You can now spot a fake account or scam on social media and refuse it.

check.q: Which of these is a warning sign of a scam on social media?
options: Pressure to act right now and pay with a gift card
A friend you know sharing a birthday photo
A local group posting a meeting time
check.why: Pressure to act now and payment by gift card are signs the FTC lists.

check.q: Someone you met online offers you a job if you first send them a code from your phone. What would you do?
options: Send money instead of the code
Refuse and never send codes to someone you only met online
check.why: Never send money, gift cards or codes to someone you have only met online.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reporting, blocking and taking a break
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Block or report an account and control how much time you spend.
This lesson builds toward: Given an unwanted post, account or habit, you will block, report or mute it and set a time limit for the app, choosing the right tool for each case.
Block stops a person from seeing your posts or contacting you. Report tells the app that an account or post breaks its rules, such as a scam, a fake account or bullying. Unfollow or mute hides someone's posts without telling them.
These buttons are usually in the three-dot menu on a post or on a person's profile. The app does not tell the person you reported them.
Social media is made to keep you scrolling. Many phones and apps have a screen time or time limit setting. Pick times to check it, and step away if posts make you feel angry or sad.
Step by step:
- Tap the three dots on the post or profile.
- Choose Report and pick the reason, or Block.
- Use Mute or Unfollow to hide posts quietly.
- In Settings, look for screen time or a daily time limit.
Words to know:
- Block: stops a person from seeing you or contacting you.
- Report: tells the app an account or post breaks its rules.
- Mute: hides someone's posts without telling them.
Try it now: Final task practice: on any post, tap the three dots and find Report, Block and Mute (do not press them unless you need to). Then check your privacy setting is still friends only.
You can now block, report or mute an account and set limits on your time.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Privacy settings Posts are still public, or anyone can follow without approval. Posts are visible only to friends or approved followers. Also limits who can message you and turns off location in posts. Following safely Followed no one, or followed an account without checking it was real. Follows one checked family member or friend and one local group or page. Explains how they checked the photo, shared friends and posts. Kind comment No comment, or the comment is unkind or shares private details. One kind, suitable comment on a post. The comment is warm and specific to the post. Report button Cannot find Report on a post or account. Finds Report in the three-dot menu on a post or account. Also finds Block and Mute and says when to use each. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Tells the app a post or account breaks its rules
check.why: Report tells the app about a scam, fake account or bullying.

check.q: A relative posts so much that you want to see less, without upsetting them. What would you do?
check.why: Mute or unfollow hides their posts without telling them.
